---
title: Chapter 8.1 Limits of Sequences of Numbers
subtitle: Calculator Explorations of Limits; Exercises 23-30
output: pdf_document
---

In Exercises 23-26, experiment with a calculator to find a value of $N$ that
will make the inequality hold for all $n > N$. Assuming that the inequality is
the one from the formal definition of the limit of a sequence, what sequence is
being considered in each case and what is its limit?

---

> _In each of these exercises we are given the convergence condition for a
> sequence and the particular $\varepsilon$ band that the tail becomes confined
> in. We are asked to find the $N$ where this sequence becomes confined in the
> band. We also want to know the direction from which the sequence approaches
> its limit._

> _We will be using R programming to solve each. We use R to find $N$ and
> include the code. The graph will also be provided for each function._

---

23. $\lvert\sqrt[n]{0.5} - 1\rvert < 10^{-3}$

```{r exercise_23, echo=TRUE}
# |0.5^(1/n) - 1| < 10^-3 -->  a_n = 0.5^(1/n), L = 1, eps <- 1e-3
n   <- 1:5000
e23 <- function(n) 0.5^(1/n)
L   <- 1
eps <- 1e-3
N <- max(which(abs(e23(n) - L) >= eps))    # 692
```

```{r exercise_23_graph, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/08-Chapter/8-01-p23.png")
```

The sequence is $a_n = \sqrt[n]{0.5}$ and the limit is $L = 1$. The sequence
approaches this limit from below and enters the lower edge $1 - 10^{-3}$ of the
band $1 \pm 10^{-3}$, and stays inside it for all $n > N = `r N`$.

---

24. $\lvert\sqrt[n]{n} - 1\rvert < 10^{-3}$

```{r exercise_24, echo=TRUE}
# |n^(1/n) - 1| < 10^-3 --> a_n = n^(1/n), L = 1, eps = 1e-3
n <- 1:20000
e24 <- function(n) n^(1/n)
L   <- 1
eps <- 1e-3
N <- max(which(abs(e24(n) - L) >= eps))
```

```{r exercise_24_graph, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/08-Chapter/8-01-p24.png")
```

Note that $a_1 = 1$ lies in the band, but $a_2$ and $a_3$ do not; what matters
is that the entire tail, $n > `r N`$, stays inside.

The sequence is $a_n = \sqrt[n]{n}$ and the limit is $L = 1$. The sequence
approaches this limit from above and enters the upper edge of the limit band $1
\pm 10^{-3}$ and stays in the band for all $n > N = `r N`$.

---

25. $(0.9)^n < 10^{-3}$

```{r exercise_25, echo=TRUE}
# |0.9^n - 0| < 10^-3 --> a_n = 0.9^n, L = 0, eps = 1e-3
n <- 1:100
e25 <- function(n) 0.9^n
L <- 0
eps <- 1e-3
N <- max(which(abs(e25(n) - L) >= eps))
```

```{r exercise_25_graph, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/08-Chapter/8-01-p25.png")
```

The sequence is $a_n = 0.9^n$ and the limit is $L = 0$. The sequence approaches
this limit from above and enters the upper edge of the limit band $0 \pm
10^{-3}$ and stays in the band for all $n > N = `r N`$.

---

26. $\frac{2^n}{n!} < 10^{-7}$

```{r exercise_26, echo=TRUE}
# |2^n / n! - 0| < 10^-7 --> a_n = 2^n / n!,  L = 0,  eps = 1e-7
n <- 1:40
e26 <- function(n) (2^n)/factorial(n)
L   <- 0
eps <- 1e-7
N <- max(which(abs(e26(n) - L) >= eps))
```

```{r exercise_26_graph, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/08-Chapter/8-01-p26.png")
```

The plot is on a log scale because the terms shrink by a factor of
$\frac{2}{n+1}$ each step. The sequence is $a_n = \frac{2^n}{n!}$ and the limit
is $L = 0$. The sequence approaches this limit from above and enters the upper
edge of the limit band $0 \pm 10^{-7}$ and stays within the band for all $n > N
= `r N`$.

---

27. __Sequences generated by Newton's method.__ Newton's method, applied to a
    differentiable function $f(x)$, begins with a starting value of $x_0$ and
    constructs from it a sequence of numbers $\{x_n\}$ that under favorable
    circumstances converges to a zero of $f$. The recursion formula for the
    sequence is
$$
x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}.
$$

a. Show that the recursion formula for $f(x) = x^2 - a, a > 0$, can be written
   as $x_{n+1} = (x_n + a / x_n) / 2$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x_n) &= x_n^2 - a \quad \quad f'(x_n) = 2x_n \\
x_{n+1} &= x_n - \frac{x_n^2 - a}{2x_n} \\
x_{n+1} &= x_n - \frac{1}{2}\left(x_n - \frac{a}{x_n}\right) \\
x_{n+1} &= x_n - \frac{1}{2}x_n + \frac{a/x_n}{2} \\
x_{n+1} &= \frac{1}{2}x_n + \frac{a/x_n}{2} \\
x_{n+1} &= \frac{x_n + a/x_n}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

b. Starting with $x_0 = 1$ and $a = 3$, calculate successive terms of the
   sequence until the display begins to repeat. What number is being
   approximated? Explain.

```{r exercise_27, echo=TRUE}
newton_seq <- function(x, a, n = 5) {
    for (i in 1:n) x <- c(x, (x[length(x)] + a / x[length(x)]) / 2)
    x
}
newton_seq(1, 3)
```

> The number being approximated is $\sqrt{3} = `r round(sqrt(3), 6)`$. If $x_n
> \to L$, then taking limits on both sides of $x_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}\left(x_n +
> \frac{3}{x_n}\right)$ gives $L = \frac{1}{2}\left(L + \frac{3}{L}\right)$, so
> $L^2 = 3$. Since $x_0 = 1 > 0$, every term is positive, so $L = \sqrt{3}$.

---

28. Repeat part (b) of Exercise 27 with $a = 2$ in place of $a = 3$

```{r exercise_28, echo=TRUE}
newton_seq(1, 2)
```

> The number being approximated is $\sqrt{2} = `r round(sqrt(2), 6)`$. Similar
> to 27(b), a limit $L$ must satisfy $L = \frac{1}{2}\left(L +
> \frac{2}{L}\right)$, so $L^2 = 2$, and since every term is positive, $L =
> \sqrt{2}$.

---

29. __A recursive definition of $\pi / 2$.__ If you start with $x_1 = 1$ and
    define the subsequent terms of $\{x_n\}$ by the rule $x_n = x_{n-1} +
    \cos x_{n-1}$, you generate a sequence that converges rapidly to $\pi/2$.
    (a) Try it. (b) Use the accompanying figure to explain why the convergence
    is so rapid.

```{r exercise_29_graph, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/08-Chapter/8-01-p29.png")
```

a. Using a recursive function to approximate $\pi/2$.

```{r exercise_29}
pi_seq <- function(x, n = 3) {
    for (i in 1:n) x <- c(x, x[length(x)] + cos(x[length(x)]))
    x
}
print(approx_pi <- pi_seq(1), digits = 15)
print(pi / 2, digits = 15)
```

> After three steps, $x_4 = `r format(approx_pi[4], digits=15)`$, which agrees with $\pi/2$ to every
> digit shown.

b. In the figure, the arc from $P = (\cos x_{n-1}, \sin x_{n-1})$ to $(0, 1)$
   has length $\frac{\pi}{2} - x_{n-1}$, and the horizontal segment from $P$ to
   the y-axis has length $\cos x_{n-1}$. Near the top of the circle the arc is
   nearly horizontal, so these two lengths are nearly equal. Adding $\cos
   x_{n-1}$ therefore takes $x_{n-1}$ almost exactly to $\frac{\pi}{2}$. More
   precisely, let $\varepsilon = \frac{\pi}{2} - x_{n-1}$. Since $\cos x_{n-1}
   = \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \varepsilon\right) = \sin\varepsilon$,

$$
x_n = \frac{\pi}{2} - \varepsilon + \sin\varepsilon,
    \qquad \frac{\pi}{2} - x_n = \varepsilon - \sin\varepsilon \approx
    \frac{\varepsilon^3}{6},
$$

> using $\sin\varepsilon = \varepsilon - \frac{\varepsilon^3}{6} + \cdots$. So
> each new error is roughly the cube of the previous one (divided by 6): the
> errors are about $0.57$, $0.031$, $4.7 \times 10^{-6}$, and then below
> machine precision. The number of correct digits roughly triples at each step,
> which is why three iterations are enough.

---

30. According to a front-page article in the December 15, 1992, issue of _The
    Wall Street Journal_, Ford Motor Company now uses about $7\frac{1}{4}$
    hours of labor to produce stampings for the average vehicle, down from an
    estimated 15 hours in 1980. The Japanese need only about $3\frac{1}{2}$
    hours. Ford's improvement since 1980 represents an average decrease of 6%
    per year. If that rate continues, then $n$ years from now Ford will use
    about

    $$
    S_n = 7.25(0.94)^n
    $$

    hours of labor to produce stampings for the average vehicle. Assuming that
    the Japanese continue to spend $3\frac{1}{2}$ hours per vehicle, how many
    more years will it take Ford to catch up? Find out two ways:

    a. Find the first term of the sequence $\{S_n\}$ that is less than or equal
       to 3.5.

```{r exercise_30_a}
n <- 1:25
f <- function(x) 7.25 * 0.94^x
Sn <- f(n)
n_cross <- which(Sn <= 3.5)[1]
x_cross <- log(3.5 / 7.25) / log(0.94)
```

> The first term with $S_n \le 3.5$ is $S_{12} \approx `r round(Sn[n_cross], 2)`$,
  so Ford catches up in about `r n_cross` years.

>  b. GRAPHER Graph $f(x) = 7.25(0.94)^x$ and use TRACE to find where the graph
      crosses the line $y=3.5$.

```{r exercise_30_b, out.width="55%", fig.align="center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/08-Chapter/8-01-p30b.png")
```

> Solving $7.25(0.94)^x = 3.5$ gives $x = \frac{\ln(3.5/7.25)}{\ln 0.94}
> \approx `r round(x_cross, 2)`$. So Ford catches up during year `r n_cross`,
> which agrees with part (a).
